cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Yu Lan Xiang strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken overnight to a light-medium oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and lightly charcoal roasted; the soft leaf is handled gently to keep its magnolia aroma.
harvest_season: Spring, roughly April into May depending on elevation; picked once, with a small autumn lot in some gardens.
appearance_dry: Long, broad, slightly loose olive-brown strips with a soft, sweet floral smell.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold to light orange, clear.
appearance_wet: Soft, broad yellow-green leaves with light red edges.
taste_profile: Soft magnolia and white-flower aroma with a gentle honeyed sweetness, a light-to-medium, creamy body and a mild, cool finish with very little astringency.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. It is one of the gentlest dancongs and one of the shortest-lived; enjoy the first five steeps and do not push it into long infusions, which only make it thin.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, spring tea lightly roasted and on sale from around June, with the village and elevation stated by serious sellers. The light roast makes it a drink-young tea: best within a year, kept sealed, and not aged.
description:
Yu Lan Xiang, magnolia fragrance, is the soft-spoken member of the Phoenix dancong family: a gentle leaf with a white-flower aroma, a creamy sweetness and almost no bite. If Ba Xian is the tea for people who like a challenge, this is the one for people who like to be comfortable.

It is one of the ten classic aroma types, named for the magnolia (yu lan) whose scent the cup recalls. It is usually described as a selection from the Fenghuang Shui Xian population on the mountains above Chaozhou, propagated by cuttings, though at least one seller calls it a natural hybrid native to Wudong. The leaf is soft, and the strain is grown from the low gardens up to the high slopes.

Makers treat it carefully. Oxidation is kept light-medium and the charcoal roast light, because the magnolia note is delicate and the leaf, being soft, scorches easily. The result is a pale gold liquor, a soft floral aroma rather than the loud perfume of Ya Shi Xiang, and a smooth, creamy texture with a gentle honey note and a mild, cooling finish.

It is an early-session tea and a short one: five good steeps, then a polite fade. Brew it with the usual dancong technique, lots of leaf, boiling water, flash pours, and resist the urge to extend the later steeps, which only thins it out. It is also one of the few dancongs that is pleasant brewed Western style in a pot, 4 g per 200 ml for a minute.

It is sold by year and should be drunk within the year, sealed and away from heat. Prices are often moderate, since the market prizes louder aromas, which makes it a good-value introduction to the gentle end of Phoenix tea. From here, Zhi Lan Xiang adds brightness and Mo Li Xiang adds a jasmine edge.
history:
Yu Lan Xiang is one of the ten aroma types of Phoenix dancong, named because its scent recalls white magnolia. It is generally placed among the selections from the Fenghuang Shui Xian population, while one seller describes it as a natural hybrid of local dancong varieties native to Wudong. A related name, Jin Yu Lan, also circulates.

Little is documented about when it was first singled out, and neither account has been settled in anything more formal than the tea trade's own writing.
